items.value: Livelihood dependence and ecosystem degradation reinforce each other, producing conflict and imbalance
items.reasoning: The passage is built on a conflict: an ecosystem cannot be used only for livelihoods, only for commerce and only for conservation at once, and deforestation for commerce causes floods, siltation and microclimatic instability while also harming the livelihoods that depend on the forest. That mutual worsening ending in conflict and imbalance is exactly option C. A is contradicted by the passage, which treats conservation as a genuine claim; B introduces fundamental rights, a legal idea the passage never raises; D demands a total stop to commercial exploitation, which the passage never advocates and in fact notes can boost national income.

Assumption I is the opposite of what the passage says: it states that in developing countries commercial exploitation has the potential to boost national income, so it does not take for granted that no country needs ecosystems for income. Assumption II brings in resource sharing between rich and poor countries, a subject the passage never touches at all. Neither is presupposed by the argument, so the answer is neither.

items.value: Timing is crucial in green technology development, because an early, gradual transition is cheaper than a late, chaotic one
items.reasoning: The passage's first three sentences set out the mechanism (steep learning curve, path dependence, solar prices collapsing 90 per cent) purely as support for its concluding claim: moving early and gradually lets economies reap the benefits without much disruption, whereas a late, more chaotic transition is costlier. That conclusion is option D. A overstates by calling economies of scale essential, when the passage names it as only one of two reasons costs fall. B generalises to all modern technological progress, far wider than the passage's subject. C confuses economies of scale with large national economies, a claim the passage never makes.

Assumption II follows the passage's own logic: it presents solar as the strongest evidence for a steep learning curve in renewable energy generally, and says an early, gradual transition happens without much disruption, so a passage reader must take it for granted that other technologies repeating the solar pattern would make the transition easier. Assumption I fails because it adds public finances, a dimension the passage never mentions, and pins the claim to India, which the passage never discusses. Since one holds and one does not, the answer is II only.

items.value: 8 numbers below 50 have the property (the multiples of 6: 6, 12, 18, 24, 30, 36, 42, 48)
items.reasoning: Write the three distinct factors as N/a, N/b, N/c, so a, b, c are also factors and 1/a + 1/b + 1/c = 1. The only solutions of that equation in natural numbers are (3,3,3), (2,4,4) and (2,3,6), and only (2,3,6) has all three different, which the question requires. So N must be divisible by 6 and the decomposition is always N = N/2 + N/3 + N/6. Below 50 the multiples of 6 are 6, 12, 18, 24, 30, 36, 42 and 48, giving 8; an exhaustive check of every N below 50 confirms exactly this list.

items.value: 4 distinct values of p + q + r are possible, namely 15, 21, 33 and 39
items.reasoning: The condition p - q = q - r means the three primes are in arithmetic progression, so their sum is 3q. Taking primes below 20 there are exactly five such progressions: (3,5,7), (3,7,11), (5,11,17), (3,11,19) and (7,13,19), with sums 15, 21, 33, 33 and 39. Two of them share the sum 33, so the number of DISTINCT sums is 4, not 5 (which is the trap that option B is designed to catch). Note the stem does not say the three primes are distinct; if p = q = r were allowed the condition becomes vacuous and 8 sums arise, which would make the answer D. The deliberate use of the word 'distinct' for the values, and the presence of 5 as a near-miss option, both point to the intended reading being three different primes, so 4 is given here.

Take p less than or equal to q less than or equal to r. Then 3/p is at least 1, so p is at most 3, and p cannot be 1. If p = 2 the rest must total 1/2, giving (2,3,6) or (2,4,4); if p = 3 the rest must total 2/3, forcing q = r = 3. So the only triples are (3,3,3), (2,4,4) and (2,3,6), whose sums are 9, 10 and 11 respectively. That is three distinct values.

items.value: X is July and Y is April
items.reasoning: Each term is obtained from the previous one by stepping back a growing number of months, subtracting 0, then 1, then 2, then 3, and so on, wrapping round the year. January minus 0 is January; minus 1 is December; minus 2 is October; minus 3 is July, so X is July; minus 4 is March; minus 5 is October (March back five months wraps to October); minus 6 is April, so Y is April; and April minus 7 is September, which matches the printed last term. Every given term is reproduced by this rule, so July and April is the answer.

items.value: Cannot be determined; the second condition is an identity and adds no information
items.reasoning: Ten per cent fewer overs than 20 is 18, so team Y's run rate is N/18. Raising a rate by 50 per cent divides the time taken by 1.5, and 18 divided by 1.5 is exactly 12. So the statement about 12 overs is automatically true for every possible N and places no constraint on the total at all. With only one unknown and no independent equation, N cannot be pinned down, which rules out 72, 144 and 216 equally.

A rise of k per cent followed by a fall of k per cent multiplies the price by (1 + k/100)(1 - k/100) = 1 - k^2/10000, which equals (10^4 - k^2)/10^4. That pair of changes happens twice, so q = p times (10^4 - k^2)^2 divided by 10^8. Rearranging gives p(10^4 - k^2)^2 = q x 10^8. Options C and D lose the squaring, and B has the wrong power of ten; a numerical check with p = 200 and k = 20, which gives q = 184.32, confirms option A exactly.

items.value: India should frame climate mitigation and adaptation strategies at the State or regional level
items.reasoning: The whole passage is a list of how challenges and opportunities differ by region, coasts facing sea level rise, drier districts facing variable monsoons, the Himalaya having unique problems, peninsular and offshore areas suited to wind power, and it closes by saying these aspects must be considered in setting goals. The pragmatic message that follows is that strategy must be region specific, which is option D. A and C are about who bears responsibility, States or the Union, a question the passage never raises. B turns the passage's premise of diversity into defeatism, the opposite of its constructive closing sentence.

Assumption I is required by the passage's own example: it says peninsular and offshore areas offer great opportunities for harnessing wind power and presents this as an opportunity for reducing emissions, which only makes sense if green energy production can be folded into mitigation strategy. Assumption II is a comparative claim the passage never makes; it treats coastal, dry and Himalayan regions alike as each having a distinctive set of challenges, without ranking any as more severely affected. So I holds and II does not.

items.value: Insecurity rather than poverty is the main economic issue that Government policy must address
items.reasoning: The passage states in its opening sentence that insecurity, more than poverty, is the most acutely felt economic problem, and closes by noting that many Government policies are actually intended to mitigate these insecurities. Option D states precisely that. A muddles the passage's careful separation of social inequality as the social problem from insecurity as the economic one. B asserts poverty as the primary cause of inequality and insecurity, a causal claim absent from the text. C calls the crisis unmanageable, which the passage contradicts by pointing to policies already aimed at it.

Assumption I is directly grounded: the passage says that besides those below the official poverty line, even those just over it face multiple economic insecurities from health risks, market fluctuations and job uncertainty. Assumption II claims that removing poverty would bring peace and social equality, but the passage keeps social inequality and economic insecurity as separate problems and explicitly ranks insecurity above poverty, so it cannot be assuming poverty eradication would settle inequality. Hence I only.

items.value: Both statements are correct: 9 cuts is the minimum and 6 pieces are unpainted
items.reasoning: To get equal pieces the cube must be divided into a x b x c parts with abc = 60, needing (a-1) + (b-1) + (c-1) cuts, so the cuts are minimised by minimising a + b + c. Checking every factorisation of 60, the smallest sum is 3 + 4 + 5 = 12, giving 2 + 3 + 4 = 9 cuts, so statement I is correct. With a 3 by 4 by 5 arrangement the pieces touching no outer face form the inner block of size (3-2) x (4-2) x (5-2) = 1 x 2 x 3 = 6, so statement II is correct too.

The operation is the hypotenuse rule: a * b is the square root of a squared plus b squared. Check both given cases: 7 and 24 give the square root of 49 + 576 = 625, which is 25, and 12 and 16 give the square root of 144 + 256 = 400, which is 20. Applying it, 16 and 63 give the square root of 256 + 3969 = 4225, which is 65.

At 16 km per litre, 2200 km needs 137.5 litres, which at Rs 90 per litre costs Rs 12375. After the 10 per cent hike petrol costs Rs 99 per litre, so the same Rs 12375 buys 12375 divided by 99 = 125 litres, which covers 125 times 16 = 2000 km. The travel must therefore fall by 2200 - 2000 = 200 km.

In every case the remainder is two less than the divisor: 3 - 2 = 1, 5 - 2 = 3, 6 - 2 = 4 and 9 - 2 = 7. So N + 2 is divisible by 3, 5, 6 and 9, that is by their LCM, 90, and N has the form 90k - 2. The smallest four-digit member needs 90k at least 1002, so k = 12 and N = 1080 - 2 = 1078. Checking directly, 1078 leaves 1, 3, 4 and 7 on division by 3, 5, 6 and 9.

In statement I the chain runs B greater than C, C less than D, D greater than E, so B and E are linked only through the small quantity C and no comparison between them follows; taking B = 5, C = 1, D = 100, E = 50 satisfies every printed relation yet leaves B smaller than E. In statement II the chain gives S = T, T at most U, U = V, so S is at most V but need not be strictly less; taking S = T = U = V = 5 with P = 6, Q = R = 5 and W = 4 satisfies every relation while S equals V. Both conclusions fail, so neither is correct.

The product runs over odd numbers only, so it has no factor of 2 and is itself odd. It does contain the factor 5 (indeed 5, 15, 25 and so on), so the product is an odd multiple of 5. Every odd multiple of 5 ends in the digit 5, so the units digit is 5.
